Act: Personal Data Protection Act 2012;

Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Act 2020
Provision context: Horizontal
Legal effect: According to Section 26, an organisation may only transfer personal data outside Singapore if it has taken appropriate steps to ensure that: 
- it will comply with the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) obligations in respect of the transferred personal data while it remains in its possession or under its control; and 
- the recipient outside of Singapore is bound by legally enforceable obligations to provide a standard of protection to the personal data transferred that is comparable to that under the PDPA. 

In this regard, “legally enforceable obligations” would include obligations imposed on the recipient: (i) under law (e.g. the recipient’s relevant national data privacy legislation); (ii) under any contract: (a) requiring the recipient to provide a standard of protection to the personal data transferred that is at least comparable to the protection under the PDPA; and (b) specifying the countries and territories to which the personal data may be transferred under the contract; (iii) under binding corporate rules (see below); or (iv) any other legally binding instrument.

An organisation will be taken to have satisfied the second requirement if the individual consents to the transfer of the personal data to the recipient in that country.

Act: Law on Electronic Data Protection No.25/NA 2017
;
Guidelines on the Implementation of the Law on Electronic Data Protection No. 2126/MoPTC
Provision context: Horizontal
Legal effect: Lao PDR does not have comprehensive data protection law. The data protection in Lao PDR mainly refers to the protection of data in electronic format. The protection can be found in specific regulations, such as the Law on Electronic Data Protection No.25/NA, Law on Prevention and Combating Cybercrime No. 61/NA, and Penal Code No. 26/NA. 

Specifically, under the Electronic Data Protection No. 25/NA, the electronic data refers to general data (data of individual, legal entities or organizations) and specific data (official/personal data that not allow individual, legal entities or organizations to access, use or disclose without permission from the owner or relevant organizations) (Articles 8-10). Additionally, in August 2018, to clarify the requirements under the Law on Electronic Data Protection, the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications issued the Guidelines on the Implementation of the Law on Electronic Data Protection No. 2126/MoPTC. The E-Data Protection Guidelines provide greater clarity on the classification of electronic data, the compliance obligations of data managers, and rules associated with regulated data protection activities. These Guidelines cover: (i) data collection; (ii) electronic data inspection; (iii) saving/storing of electronic data; (iv) maintaining electronic data; (v) using and disseminating electronic data; (vi) transmission and transfer of electronic data; (vii) access to electronic data; (viii) amending and updating electronic data; and (ix) deletion of electronic data.

Lao PDR has no comprehensive data protection framework that applies universally across all sectors. Instead, the country has adopted a more sector-specific (sectoral) approach to data protection. The Law on Electronic Data Protection (2017) does provide guidelines for the handling and processing of sensitive data, such as personal, financial, and medical information, but these rules are often integrated into other sectoral regulations. Lao PDR is still in the process of developing a more robust data protection regime, with ongoing efforts to enhance the legal and institutional framework for data security​ (ESCAP-2022-PB-Readiness)​ (Implementation Guide). However, the country has not yet enacted a comprehensive, cross-sectoral data protection law similar to the GDPR or California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA), which would apply universally across all sectors.

;
Bank Indonesia Regulation No. 22/23/PBI/2020 on Payment Systems 2020
Provision context: Financial sector
Legal effect: Financial Services Authority (OJK) Regulation No.38/POJK.03/2016 requires banks to store and process data  in data centers or disaster recovery centers within territory of Indonesia. Financial Services Authority (OJK) Regulation No.38/POJK.03/2016, which required banks to store and process data in data centers or disaster recovery centers within the territory of Indonesia, has been revoked and replaced by OJK Regulation No.11/POJK.03/2022. This new regulation explicitly addresses the requirements for data storage and processing by banks, including the possibility of placing data centers or disaster recovery centers outside Indonesia under certain conditions. 

Article 35:
- Paragraph (1): Banks are required to place their data centers and disaster recovery centers within the territory of Indonesia.
- Paragraph (2): Banks may place their data centers and/or disaster recovery centers outside Indonesia, but only with prior approval from the Financial Services Authority (OJK).
- Paragraph (3): Specifies the criteria for systems that can be placed outside Indonesia, such as systems for global integrated analysis, risk management, anti-money laundering, and others.

Article 72: Explicitly revokes OJK Regulation No.38/POJK.03/2016 and its amendment (OJK Regulation No.13/POJK.03/2020), stating that they are no longer valid as of the effective date of OJK Regulation No.11/POJK.03/2022.

Bank Indonesia Regulation No.22/23/PBI/2020 requires domestic processing of initiation-authorization-clearing-settlements phases of payment transactions for instruments issued by Indonesia's payment service provider and conducted within the territory of the Republic of Indonesia. Indonesia opens the possibility of such payment transactions to be processed outside of Indonesian territory for the purpose of global reconciliation, integrated risk management system/anti-money laundering. However, this is subject to Bank Indonesia's approval. Banks are required to carry out IT-based transaction processing in Indonesia, either independently or by third parties. Australia's Cyber Security is guided through the 2023-2030 Australian Cyber Security Strategy, which includes a roadmap for new legislation and standards.
